Chapter 10: Emotion, Suffering, and the Inner Lives of Animals.
For centuries, people have asked—do animals really feel emotions? Some folks have argued that animals are just like machines, only reacting to pain or pleasure without any real feelings. But, if you’ve ever shared your life with a dog, watched an elephant mourn, or seen a mother bird fiercely guard her nest, you know there’s more to the story.
Emotions are part of an animal’s everyday life. Picture a young elephant in the wild who’s just lost her mother. She lingers near the spot for days, gently touching the bones with her trunk, refusing to eat. Other elephants gather close, offering soft touches and low rumbles, almost like they’re comforting her. That grief? It’s impossible to miss—and honestly, it’s not so different from what we feel in moments of loss.
But it’s not all sadness. Joy is everywhere in the animal world. Dolphins leap and spin in the waves, playing games that don’t seem to have any real purpose. Ravens slide down snowy rooftops, cackling with what sure looks like delight. Even rats, when they’re tickled, let out tiny, high-pitched chirps—almost like laughter, as researchers have discovered.
Animals feel fear, anger, jealousy, and affection too. These emotions shape their choices, the friendships they build, and the risks they’re willing to take. There’s this one experiment where monkeys were given a choice: help a friend escape a mild shock or keep a treat for themselves. Most chose to help, even if it meant missing out on something tasty. That urge to care, protect, and comfort? It’s not just a human thing.
But let’s not forget—the flip side of emotions is suffering. When animals in captivity are cut off from stimulation or companionship, many show signs of depression or anxiety. Think of the pacing, self-harm, or withdrawal you sometimes see in zoos or labs. These aren’t just odd habits. They’re cries for help—proof that animals’ emotional needs are just as real as their physical ones.
Seeing animals this way isn’t only about science—it’s about empathy. It invites us to recognize animals as individuals, each with their own joys and heartaches, hopes and fears.
And honestly, the more we discover, the harder it is to draw a sharp line between what humans feel and what animals experience. This world is full of beating hearts, each with its own rhythm—each one capable of love, and yes, of loss.
